summary: This document extends the way Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) carries multicast traffic, which earlier RFCs 4761 and 4762 handled with unicast tunnels. Those tunnels can waste bandwidth when a lot of multicast data is sent. It describes solutions to overcome a subset of those limits.

plainLanguage.summary: A virtual private LAN service connects a customer's sites as if they were on one local network. When one of those sites sends a multicast packet, the usual way to deliver it is to copy it once for every other site and send each copy down its own tunnel. This document describes an alternative: a single shared tree in the provider's own network, so one copy travels and is copied only where it has to be.

subtitle: How VPLS carries multicast on shared trees in the provider network instead of copying every packet to every edge router.

tldr.problem: VPLS multicast as defined in RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 uses ingress replication, where the ingress router copies each multicast or broadcast packet to every other edge router over unicast tunnels, which wastes bandwidth when traffic is heavy.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress Provider Edge router sends the packets down a point-to-multipoint tree in the provider network, signalled by RSVP-TE or mLDP. One tree can serve one or several VPLS instances, and BGP announces which tree carries what.
tldr.outcome: Heavy multicast uses far less core bandwidth, at the cost of tree state in the provider network. High-bandwidth streams can be moved to Selective trees that reach only the routers that have receivers.

today: RFC 7117 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the VPLS specifications RFC 4761 and RFC 4762.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 describe a solution for VPLS multicast and broadcast that relies on pseudowires transported over unicast point-to-point RSVP Traffic Engineering or multipoint-to-point LDP Label Switched Paths. In this document that solution is called ingress replication.

With ingress replication, when an ingress Provider Edge (PE) of a given VPLS instance receives a multicast or broadcast packet from one of the Customer Edges that belong to that instance, the ingress PE replicates the packet for each egress PE that belongs to that instance, and sends the packet to each such egress PE using unicast tunnels.

That solution has limitations for certain VPLS multicast traffic profiles. It can result in highly non-optimal bandwidth utilisation in the MPLS network when a large amount of multicast traffic is to be transported. Ingress replication may be an acceptable model when the bandwidth of the multicast traffic is low, or when only a small number of replications is performed on each outgoing interface for a particular VPLS customer multicast stream. Where that is not the case, it is desirable to use multicast trees in the service provider network to transmit VPLS multicast and broadcast packets.

This document therefore describes procedures for using MPLS point-to-multipoint Label Switched Paths in the service provider network to transport VPLS multicast and broadcast packets, where these LSPs are signalled by either P2MP RSVP-TE or Multipoint LDP. The procedures apply to both RFC 4761 and RFC 4762.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way copies every multicast packet once for each customer site and sends each copy down its own tunnel. That is fine for light traffic and wasteful for heavy traffic.

sections.title: Terminology and Tree Types
sections.content:
The document uses terminology from RFC 4761 and RFC 4762. It refers to the various auto-discovery routes as 'A-D routes'. It uses the prefix 'C' for customer control or data packets and 'P' for provider control or data packets, and abbreviates an IP multicast source and group tuple as (S, G).

An Inclusive tree is a single multicast distribution tree in the service provider network that carries all the multicast traffic from one VPLS instance on a given PE. An Aggregate Inclusive tree is a single multicast distribution tree in the service provider network that carries all the multicast traffic from more than one VPLS instance on a given PE.

A Selective tree is a single multicast distribution tree in the service provider network that carries multicast traffic belonging only to a specified set of IP multicast streams, all of which belong to the same VPLS instance on a given PE. A Selective tree differs from an Inclusive tree in that it may reach a subset of the PEs reached by an Inclusive tree. An Aggregate Selective tree is a single multicast distribution tree in the service provider network that carries multicast traffic belonging only to a specified set of IP multicast streams, all of which belong to more than one VPLS instance on a given PE.
sections.plainLanguage: An Inclusive tree carries everything from a customer network. A Selective tree carries only named multicast streams and reaches only the routers that have receivers for them. Either kind can be shared between several customer networks.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The procedures provide mechanisms that allow a single multicast distribution tree in the service provider network to carry all the multicast traffic from one or more VPLS sites connected to a given PE, irrespective of whether those sites belong to the same or different VPLS instances. The document also provides procedures by which a single tree can carry traffic belonging only to a specified set of IP multicast streams. By default, multicast traffic is carried on an Inclusive tree, while traffic from some specific IP multicast streams, for example high-bandwidth streams, can be carried on a Selective tree. The document covers the use of Selective trees only for carrying IP multicast streams.

Unicast packets destined to unknown Media Access Control addresses in a given VPLS instance are flooded to the remote PEs participating in that instance. This flooding may still use ingress replication, or may use the procedures in this document to optimise flooding across the service provider core.

Using multicast trees in the service provider network is beneficial when the bandwidth of the multicast traffic is high, or when it is desirable to reduce the number of copies of a multicast packet transmitted on a given link. The benefit comes at the cost of state in the service provider network to build the multicast trees and overhead to maintain that state.

Auto-discovery uses the BGP-based procedures of RFC 4761 and RFC 6074 to discover VPLS membership. A PE that belongs to a particular VPLS instance announces a BGP NLRI identifying the Virtual Switch Instance, built from the Route Distinguisher and the VPLS Edge Device Identifier tuple. The root PE of a P2MP LSP discovers the other PEs that have membership of each VPLS instance and includes them as leaves in the tree.

Aggregation is the ability to carry the traffic of more than one VPLS on the same tree. It lets the service provider place a bound on the amount of multicast tree forwarding and control plane state that the provider routers must hold. The number of trees a PE is the root of is proportional to the number of VPLS instances on the PE divided by the Aggregation Factor, so the state does not grow linearly with the number of VPLS instances. Aggregation needs a mechanism for the egresses to demultiplex the traffic, so upstream-assigned labels are assigned and distributed by the root of the aggregate tree. That requires two MPLS labels in the label stack, which introduces no new implications on MTU, since even VPLS multicast supported by ingress replication requires two MPLS labels.

For traffic between different autonomous systems, the document defines four models, options (a), (b), (c) and (e). Options (a), (b) and (c) are similar to methods in the 'Multi-AS VPLS' section of RFC 4761. For options (a) and (b), inter-AS VPLS service can be offered without a single P-multicast tree spanning multiple autonomous systems. For option (c), the service is offered by requiring a single P-multicast tree to span multiple autonomous systems, because the Autonomous System Border Routers do not exchange BGP-VPLS NLRI or A-D routes. Option (e) can be seen as a variant of option (a).
sections.plainLanguage: The tree is built from information the routers already exchange over BGP, so a provider does not have to configure every site by hand. Sharing one tree between several customer networks keeps the state in the provider routers from growing with the number of customers.

sections.title: Demultiplexing P-Multicast Tree Traffic
sections.content:
Demultiplexing received VPLS traffic requires the receiving PE to determine which VPLS instance the packet belongs to. The egress PE can then perform a VPLS lookup to forward the packet further. It also requires the egress PE to determine the identity of the ingress PE for MAC learning.

When a P-multicast tree is mapped to only one VPLS, determining the tree on which the packet arrived is enough to determine the VPLS instance. The tree is determined from the tree encapsulation: if MPLS encapsulation is used, for example with RSVP-TE P2MP LSPs, the outer MPLS label is used. Penultimate Hop Popping MUST be disabled on the MPLS LSP.

When traffic belonging to multiple VPLS instances is carried on the same tree, an inner label determines the VPLS the packet is intended for. The ingress PE uses this label as the inner label when encapsulating a customer multicast data packet, and each egress PE must be able to associate the inner label with the same VPLS. Upstream-assigned labels MUST be used in this case, so the inner label is assigned by the ingress PE. When the egress PE receives a packet over an aggregate tree, the outer encapsulation, the outer MPLS label in the case of MPLS P2MP LSPs, specifies the label space in which to perform the inner-label lookup, and the same label space MUST be used by the egress PE for all P-multicast trees that have the same root. The egress PE MUST NOT advertise IMPLICIT NULL or EXPLICIT NULL for that tree once it is known that the tree is bound to one or more VPLS instances.
sections.plainLanguage: When one tree carries several customer networks, the outer label says which tree the packet arrived on and the inner label says which customer network it belongs to. The receiving router uses the outer label to pick the right table for the inner one.

sections.title: Establishing P-Multicast Trees
sections.content:
The document supports only P2MP P-multicast trees in which egress PEs can identify the ingress PE to perform MAC learning. An implementation that supports this document MUST support RSVP-TE P2MP LSPs and mLDP P2MP LSPs.

For both, the LSP MUST be signalled with Penultimate Hop Popping off and with a non-special-purpose MPLS label, because an egress PE MUST NOT advertise IMPLICIT NULL or EXPLICIT NULL for a P2MP LSP carrying traffic for one or more VPLS instances. The egress PE needs the MPLS label it advertises to its upstream neighbour to determine the P2MP LSP on which a customer multicast data packet arrived. The egress PE also needs to identify the ingress PE to perform MAC learning, and determining the P2MP LSP is enough for that, because the ingress PE is the root of the P2MP LSP. The egress PE relies on receiving the PMSI Tunnel attribute in BGP to determine the VPLS instance to P2MP LSP mapping.

With RSVP-TE P2MP LSPs, the procedures of RFC 4875 are used to signal the LSP, and the root of the P2MP LSP discovers the leaves. The mapping from P2MP TE LSP to VPLS is learned at the egress PEs from BGP advertisements, which must include the P2MP TE LSP identifier as the P-multicast tree identifier. That identifier contains the type of the tunnel, set to RSVP-TE P2MP LSP, and the RSVP-TE P2MP LSP's SESSION Object. If the egress PE already has RSVP-TE state for the P2MP TE LSP, it MUST begin to assign an MPLS label from the non-special-purpose label range and signal it to the previous hop, and it MUST create forwarding state. If it does not yet have that state, it MUST retain the mapping and create the state when the signalling arrives. If the signalling completes before a given egress PE learns the VPLS binding, the PE MUST discard any traffic received on that LSP until the binding is received.

Receiver-initiated P2MP LSPs can also be used, signalled with the mLDP procedures of RFC 6388. The LSP is signalled once the leaves receive the LDP FEC for the tree from the root, and the tree identifier carries the type of the tunnel, set to LDP P2MP LSP, and the LDP P2MP FEC including an identifier generated by the root. Each egress PE SHOULD join the P2MP MPLS tree by sending LDP label mapping messages for that FEC.

An Aggregate Inclusive tree or an Aggregate Selective tree MUST use MPLS encapsulation, as described in RFC 5332.
sections.plainLanguage: Two signalling systems can build the tree, RSVP-TE and mLDP, and an implementation must support both. The receiving router keeps a normal MPLS label for the tree, so it can tell which tree a packet came in on, and it learns from BGP which customer networks that tree serves.

sections.title: BGP Extensions
sections.content:
Inclusive and Selective P-multicast tree advertisements carry the P-multicast tree identifier, and the document reuses the BGP attribute called 'PMSI_TUNNEL' that is defined in RFC 6514 for that purpose. Only four Tunnel Types are supported when the attribute is carried in VPLS A-D or VPLS S-PMSI A-D routes: 0 for no tunnel information present, 1 for an RSVP-TE P2MP LSP, 2 for an LDP P2MP LSP, and 6 for ingress replication.

The document defines a new BGP NLRI called the 'MCAST-VPLS NLRI'. It has three parts: a Route Type field of 1 octet, a Length field of 1 octet giving the length in octets of the route type specific field, and the route type specific field itself. Two route types are defined: 3 for a Selective Tree A-D route, and 4 for a Leaf A-D route. The MCAST-VPLS NLRI is carried in BGP using Multiprotocol Extensions with an Address Family Identifier of 25, the L2VPN AFI, and a Subsequent Address Family Identifier of MCAST-VPLS. Two BGP speakers must use the Capabilities Advertisement to confirm that both can process such NLRI, with capability code 1 and an AFI of 25.

The route type specific field of an S-PMSI A-D route holds a Route Distinguisher of 8 octets, a Multicast Source Length of 1 octet followed by the Multicast Source, a Multicast Group Length of 1 octet followed by the Multicast Group, and the originating router's IP address. The length field is 32 for an IPv4 multicast source and 128 for an IPv6 one, and may be 0 to indicate a wildcard; the same applies to the group. The Length field of the NLRI is 22 bytes when the source and group are IPv4 and the originating router's address is IPv4, 34 when the address is IPv6, 46 when the source and group are IPv6 and the address is IPv4, and 58 when all three are IPv6. The route type specific field of a Leaf A-D route holds a variable-length Route Key followed by the originating router's IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: The tree binding is carried over BGP in a new kind of route. The route says which tree, which customer networks and which multicast streams are on it, so every router in the tree learns where to send the traffic.

sections.title: Data Forwarding
sections.content:
When several VPLS instances are mapped to a P2MP LSP, the packet carries an MPLS Tree Label above a VPLS Label, above the customer Ethernet header, IP header and payload. When the ingress PE receives a packet, it determines the VPLS instance associated with the packet using the procedures of RFC 4761 and RFC 4762. If the packet is an IP multicast packet and the ingress PE uses an Aggregate Selective tree for the (C-S, C-G) carried in the packet, the ingress PE pushes the VPLS Label for that VPLS instance and the MPLS Tree Label for the Aggregate Selective tree, and sends the packet over the P2MP LSP associated with that tree. Otherwise, if the ingress PE does not use an Aggregate Selective tree for that stream, or the packet is non-IP multicast or broadcast, it pushes the VPLS Label and the MPLS Tree Label of the Aggregate Inclusive tree and sends the packet over that tree's P2MP LSP.

The egress PE looks up the outer MPLS tree label, which determines the MPLS forwarding table in which to look up the inner MPLS label, the VPLS label. That table is specific to the tree label space. The inner label is unique within the context of the root of the tree, so to identify a particular VPLS unambiguously a node needs both the VPLS label and the context in which that label is unique, which is the outer MPLS label. The outer label is popped, the lookup of the resulting label determines the VSI in which the egress PE does the customer multicast data packet lookup, the inner label is popped, and the packet is sent to the VSI for multicast data forwarding. When a single VPLS instance is mapped to a P2MP LSP, only the MPLS Tree Label is used and the egress PE looks it up directly to find the VSI.

Section 12 of the RFC then sets out which tree each packet uses. If the destination MAC address of a VPLS packet is a multicast address, a P-multicast tree SHOULD be used if possible: if the packet is an IP multicast packet and a Selective tree exists for that multicast stream, the Selective tree MUST be used; otherwise, if a Selective tree exists for the VPLS, it SHOULD be used; otherwise, if an Inclusive tree exists, it SHOULD be used. Broadcast packets are flooded, preferentially over a Selective tree and then over an Inclusive tree, and otherwise with the procedures of RFC 4761 or RFC 4762. A unicast packet whose MAC address has not been learned MUST be sent to all PEs in the VPLS, preferably over an Inclusive tree or a Selective tree bound to all sources and groups, and the receiving PEs must be able to perform MAC address learning for packets received on a multicast tree. An implementation SHOULD support transporting unknown unicast traffic over Inclusive trees and MUST support MAC address learning for packets received on a P-multicast tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet gets two labels on the way through the provider network: the outer one names the tree, the inner one names the customer network. The receiving router reads them in that order and hands the packet to the right customer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 apply, and this section adds more. There are two aspects to achieving data privacy and protecting against denial-of-service attacks in a VPLS: securing the control plane and protecting the forwarding path. Compromise of the control plane could result in a PE sending multicast data belonging to some VPLS to another VPLS, black-holing VPLS multicast data, or even sending it to an eavesdropper. It could also provide opportunities for unauthorised VPLS multicast usage, for example exploiting traffic replication within a multicast tree to amplify a denial-of-service attack.

The mechanisms in this document use BGP for the control plane, so techniques such as those in RFC 5925 help authenticate BGP messages, making it harder to spoof updates, which could divert VPLS traffic to the wrong VPLS, or withdrawals, which are denial-of-service attacks. In the multi-AS methods this also means protecting the inter-AS BGP sessions between the ASBRs, the PEs, or the Route Reflectors. Those techniques will not keep MPLS labels private: knowing the labels lets an eavesdropper read VPLS traffic. That requires access to the data path within a service provider network, which is assumed to be composed of trusted nodes and links.

One of the requirements for protecting the data plane is that MPLS labels be accepted only from valid interfaces, both for labels associated with P2MP LSPs and for upstream-assigned MPLS labels. For a PE, valid interfaces comprise links from other routers in the PE's own AS. For an ASBR, valid interfaces comprise links from other routers in the ASBR's own AS, and links from other ASBRs in autonomous systems that have instances of a given VPLS. It is especially important in the case of multi-AS VPLS instances that one accept VPLS packets only from valid interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the risk is in the control plane, where an attacker could redirect one customer's multicast to another. Authenticating the BGP sessions helps. The document also insists that routers only accept MPLS labels from links they trust.

viz.caption: MOVING A STREAM TO A SELECTIVE TREE (RFC 7117, SECTION 8.1)

items.title: Announce the binding
items.text: The source PE announces the mapping of the (C-S, C-G) streams to the Selective tree to the other PEs using BGP.

items.title: Set up the forwarding path
items.text: After the announcement, egress PEs with receivers install the demultiplexing entries for the top MPLS label or the inner label.

items.title: Wait for the switchover
items.text: The source PE waits for a switchover delay before sending the stream on the Selective tree, and the delay should be configurable.

items.title: Never both
items.text: In no case is any (C-S, C-G) packet sent on both the Selective and the Inclusive tree.
